title: Finance & Banking Questions
summary: Real questions from investment banking, corporate finance, credit, and wealth management interviews — plus the technical and ethics questions that actually trip candidates up.

sections.heading: Walk me through your resume.
sections.body:
This is the opener in almost every finance interview, and it's the one candidates prepare for least — even though it's the most predictable question in the room. The interviewer already has your resume in front of them. They're not asking for a recitation; they're testing whether you can tell a coherent story about your own decisions in under 90 seconds without rambling.

Structure it in three beats:
- Where you started and why — one sentence, don't over-explain a major you picked at 19
- Two or three experiences that build on each other, each tied to a skill the desk actually needs: modeling, client contact, accuracy under time pressure
- A closing line that connects directly to why you're sitting in this specific seat, not "finance" in the abstract

If you're doing several first-rounds in the same week, name the firm explicitly in your last line — it signals the answer wasn't copy-pasted. Time yourself out loud. The most common failure isn't a weak story, it's a six-minute answer that buries the one interesting thing about you under ten minutes of GPA and club titles.

sections.heading: Why do you want to work here specifically?
sections.body:
A generic answer here — "great culture," "strong deal flow," "smart people" — tells the interviewer you sent the same answer to twenty firms. This question is a research check disguised as a motivation question.

Come in with two concrete, firm-specific reference points, not one vague impression:
- A transaction or deal the group actually closed in the last 12–18 months that you can speak to knowledgeably (what made it interesting, not just that it happened)
- Something you learned from a real conversation — a coffee chat, an info session, an alum — that you can attribute to a person or a specific detail, not "I spoke with someone who said it was great"

Then connect it back to you: why does that specific thing matter given what you're trying to build in your career. Skip the sentence about "the people I met were so passionate" — every candidate says it, and interviewers have heard it in every single round this cycle. Specificity is the entire differentiator on this question.

sections.heading: Why finance — and why now, if you're coming from somewhere else?
sections.body:
"Why finance" from a traditional candidate and "why now" from a career-switcher are really the same question with different failure modes.

For a straight-line candidate, the trap is reciting textbook motivations ("I love the intersection of numbers and strategy"). Ground it instead in a specific moment: a project, a class, an internship task where you actually enjoyed the mechanics of the work — building the model, not just the idea of finance.

For a switcher (ex-military, consulting, engineering, another industry), the interviewer is really asking "will you actually stay, or is this a phase." Address it directly rather than hoping they don't notice the gap:
- Name what specifically pulled you — a transaction you followed, a skill gap you felt in your old role, a mentor conversation
- Show you've done something about it already — coursework, a certification, informational interviews, a related project — not just decided to apply
- Don't apologize for the switch or over-explain the old job; one sentence of context is enough

Both versions fail the same way: talking about the industry in general terms instead of your own specific pull toward it.

sections.heading: Walk me through how you'd build a DCF.
sections.body:
This is a technical question, but the interviewer is grading your ability to explain a process cleanly under pressure as much as the mechanics themselves. Walk it in order, out loud, without backtracking:

- Project unlevered free cash flow (EBIT × (1 − tax rate) + D&A − CapEx − change in net working capital) for a forecast period, typically 5–10 years
- Discount each year's cash flow back to present value using the weighted average cost of capital (WACC)
- Calculate a terminal value at the end of the forecast period — either the perpetuity growth method (final year FCF × (1+g) / (WACC − g)) or an exit multiple applied to a terminal-year metric like EBITDA — and discount that back too
- Sum the discounted cash flows and discounted terminal value to get enterprise value
- Subtract net debt (and preferred stock, minority interest) to bridge to equity value, then divide by diluted shares for a per-share value

The strongest close to this answer isn't reciting the formula faster — it's volunteering the sensitivity: "this is very sensitive to the terminal growth rate and WACC assumptions, so I'd always pair it with a sensitivity table and a comps cross-check rather than presenting one number as the answer." That one sentence signals you understand DCF's real-world limitations, not just its algebra.

sections.heading: What's the difference between enterprise value and equity value?
sections.body:
Equity value is what the common shareholders' stake in the business is worth — market cap, essentially. Enterprise value is the value of the entire operating business to all capital providers: equity holders, debt holders, and preferred holders combined, net of cash the business doesn't need to run its operations.

The bridge: Enterprise Value = Equity Value + Total Debt + Preferred Stock + Minority Interest − Cash & Cash Equivalents.

Use a real number to show you can apply it, not just recite it: "If a company has a $500M market cap, $150M of debt, and $40M of cash, its enterprise value is roughly $610M — that $610M is what an acquirer would effectively have to fund to buy the whole capital structure and retire the debt."

Then explain why the distinction matters practically: EV is capital-structure-neutral, so you use it for multiples like EV/EBITDA or EV/Revenue when comparing companies with different debt loads. Equity value is what you use for per-share metrics like P/E, since EPS is already a post-interest, post-tax number that belongs to shareholders alone. Mixing the two up — using equity value with EBITDA, for example — is one of the fastest ways to lose credibility in a technical round.

sections.heading: Pitch me a stock or an investment idea.
sections.body:
The single biggest mistake here is picking a name you don't actually follow. Interviewers will push on the numbers, and "I read about it recently" collapses in the first follow-up question. Pick something you've genuinely tracked, even if it's less exciting than the obvious mega-cap.

Structure the pitch in five parts, in this order:
- Thesis in one sentence: what the market is missing or mispricing, stated plainly, not "this is a good company"
- The variant view: why you believe something the consensus doesn't — a mispriced risk, an underappreciated growth driver, a structural change the market hasn't caught up to
- Catalyst: what happens, and roughly when, that closes the gap between price and value
- Valuation support: a specific multiple or target price, with the comp set or method you used to get there
- Key risk to the thesis, and what would make you exit or reconsider the position

Close with the risk, not the upside — it shows you're not just excited about a story, you've actually stress-tested it. An interviewer who asks "what's your biggest concern with this?" and gets a real answer instead of a shrug is far more convinced than one who hears a flawless-sounding pitch with no acknowledged downside.

sections.heading: Tell me about a time you caught a mistake — yours or someone else's — before it caused a real problem.
sections.body:
Finance interviewers ask this because the job is full of numbers that look fine until you check the second decimal, and because catching a senior person's error tactfully is its own skill separate from catching your own.

If the mistake was yours: describe what tipped you off (a number that didn't tie between two tabs, a check figure that didn't foot, a sanity check against a public comp that felt off), what you did the moment you noticed it, and how you made sure it didn't recur — a new check you added to your process, not just "I was more careful after that."

If the mistake was someone more senior's: this is the version worth rehearsing carefully, because the how matters as much as the what. Describe verifying you were right before saying anything (re-deriving the number independently, not just eyeballing it), then flagging it privately and factually rather than publicly or with any "gotcha" energy — "I noticed the WACC in tab 3 doesn't match what we used in the sensitivity table, wanted to flag before this goes out" lands completely differently than pointing out someone was wrong. End with the outcome: what got fixed, and that the relationship stayed intact afterward.

sections.heading: Tell me about a time you had to deliver under a tight deadline with limited information.
sections.body:
This question is really about stamina and triage, and finance interviewers ask it because the culture runs on last-minute changes — an MD tweaks the peer set at 9pm before a 7am pitch, a client meeting gets moved up a day, a live deal needs a revised set of numbers overnight.

Pick a specific, real example with a concrete timeline, not a vague "we were busy" story. Name what changed, when, and what the hard deadline actually was. Then show your triage logic: what you did first (often: figure out exactly what's actually needed for the deadline versus what would be nice to have), what you deprioritized on purpose, and who you looped in rather than silently grinding through alone.

Land on the result with a specific detail — the deck went out on time and the client comment the next day was about content, not errors; or you flagged early that the ask wasn't feasible in the window and got the deadline adjusted instead of quietly failing at 2am. Don't use this answer to complain about hours — a version of this story that's secretly about how hard you worked, rather than how you stayed accurate and organized under pressure, reads as a complaint rather than a strength.

sections.heading: Describe a time you had to explain a technical or financial concept to someone without a finance background.
sections.body:
This tests whether you can translate, which matters constantly in client-facing and cross-functional finance roles — a business owner doesn't want a definition of EBITDA, they want to know what it means for their loan.

Give a specific audience and a specific method you used to simplify, not just "I broke it down for them." Strong versions of this answer usually include one concrete technique: an analogy that mapped the concept to something the person already understood, a one-page visual instead of a spreadsheet, or reframing a metric in terms of a decision ("this ratio tells us whether the company can cover its debt payments this year") instead of its formula.

Include how you checked they actually understood — asking them to restate it back in their own words, or watching what question they asked next — rather than just assuming your explanation landed. Close with the outcome: a decision that got made faster or more confidently because the concept was actually understood, not just delivered.

sections.heading: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a manager's or senior colleague's numbers or approach.
sections.body:
This tests two things at once: whether you have enough technical conviction to push back at all, and whether you can do it without damaging the relationship or the deal.

Describe the specific disagreement concretely — a growth assumption you thought was too aggressive, a comp you thought didn't belong in the set, a discount rate that seemed off given the risk profile. Then show your approach to raising it: you came with your own numbers already worked through, not just a gut feeling; you framed it as a question rather than a correction ("I ran it with a slightly lower terminal growth rate and got a meaningfully different value — can I walk you through the assumption?"); and you picked the right moment and setting, not mid-client-call or in front of the team.

Be honest about the resolution, including if you didn't get your way. "They walked me through why they'd chosen that assumption, and once I saw the deal context I hadn't had visibility into, it made sense" is a completely legitimate ending — it shows you can advocate for your view and still update when you get more information. An answer where you were simply right and everyone agreed reads as either cherry-picked or oblivious to how these conversations actually go.

sections.heading: How do you handle multiple deadlines that land at the same time?
sections.body:
Interviewers use this to see whether you have an actual triage method or just work longer hours when things pile up. A real framework beats a vague "I prioritize well" every time.

Describe how you sort competing work — by hard external deadline versus internal flexibility, by who's blocked waiting on you versus who has slack, by what's reversible versus what isn't. Then give a specific real example: two pitch books due the same morning, or a live deal request landing the same afternoon as client-call prep. Walk through exactly how you sequenced it and, critically, how you communicated the sequencing upward — telling a senior person "I have X due at the same time, I'm planning to do Y first because Z, flag me if that's wrong" is itself the skill being tested, not just the task-juggling.

Avoid framing this as purely a personal-productivity story (color-coded to-do lists, a specific app). The interviewer wants to see judgment about what matters most and comfort surfacing tradeoffs to the people above you, not a time-management system.

sections.heading: Tell me about a difficult client or colleague and how you handled it.
sections.body:
The trap here is venting — a story that's really just about how unreasonable the other person was. Interviewers are listening for what you adjusted, not for validation that you were the reasonable one.

Pick a specific, real friction point: a client who was unresponsive right before a deadline, a colleague who pushed back hard on your numbers, a stakeholder who kept changing requirements. Describe the friction factually and briefly — don't dwell on it or characterize the other person negatively — then spend most of the answer on what you changed about your own approach: adjusting your communication style, over-communicating status to a client who'd gone quiet instead of assuming the worst, or finding the actual underlying concern behind a colleague's pushback instead of just defending your position harder.

Close with the outcome, and if the relationship genuinely improved afterward, say so specifically — "we ended up having a standing 15-minute check-in that fixed most of the back-and-forth" is a much stronger ending than "it eventually worked out."

sections.heading: Tell me about a time you had to deliver bad news to a client or an internal stakeholder.
sections.body:
This comes up constantly in finance — a deal timeline slipping, a valuation coming in below what a client hoped, a financing falling through, a number in a report that's worse than forecast. The question tests whether you can be direct without being either cold or evasive.

Describe the specific bad news and why it happened, briefly and honestly — don't spend the whole answer on the backstory. Then focus on how you delivered it: as early as possible once you knew, rather than hoping the situation would improve; directly, without burying it in qualifiers; and paired with next steps or options, not just the problem on its own. "The comps came in lower than the range we'd originally discussed, here's why, and here are two ways we could still get to a number you'd be comfortable with" is a fundamentally different conversation than just announcing the bad number.

If the person reacted poorly, it's fine to say so — "the client was frustrated, understandably" — as long as you follow with how you handled that reaction: staying factual, giving them space, following up in writing so there was no ambiguity about what was said.

sections.heading: What would you do if you were asked to do something you weren't comfortable with — ethically or from a compliance standpoint?
sections.body:
Finance and banking interviewers ask a version of this because the regulatory environment is real and specific — MNPI, AML rules, client conflicts, accurate representation of numbers in materials that go to clients or regulators. They're not looking for a speech about integrity; they're checking that you'd actually do something sensible in the moment rather than freeze, comply silently, or overreact.

Walk through a plausible, specific scenario rather than speaking in the abstract — being asked to include a number in a pitch you couldn't independently support, being asked to backdate or adjust a document, or realizing partway through a project that you might be working with information you shouldn't have. Then give a concrete sequence:
- Ask clarifying questions first — often what looks like a red flag has an explanation you're missing, and assuming bad intent immediately can damage a relationship over a misunderstanding
- If it still doesn't sit right after that, escalate through the actual right channel — a direct manager, or compliance if it's the manager themselves — rather than refusing unilaterally or going around them to someone else first
- Be willing to say plainly that you would not personally complete a request you believed was actually improper, even if it caused short-term friction

Keep the tone matter-of-fact rather than self-righteous — the interviewer wants to hear "here's what I'd actually do," not a values monologue. A calm, procedural answer reads as far more credible than an impassioned one.
